title: Wendell and the Postcards
premise: Oscar Eastwick, a former piano prodigy who fled the conservatory after a scandal she has never explained, returns years later as a janitor, hiding behind a practiced smile. When she hears an unrecorded song — one only her late mentor's circle ever knew — playing on the radio, she realizes someone is leaking the dead woman's unpublished work, and the trail leads through Wendell, a gentle, obsessive postman who has spent a decade delivering postcards to a mother whose memory is dissolving. Together they trace the song's journey, uncovering that Oscar's own testimony, given under pressure long ago, destroyed the mentor and buried the truth. The ending: Oscar publicly translates the 'untranslatable sentence' — her recantation — at a memorial concert, losing her anonymity but gaining a found family in Wendell and the mentor's surviving students, while the mother's memory, preserved in postcards, is finally honored.
about_author: Odile Zhou is a former conservatory librarian who left music to write about the people who sweep the stages. She lives above a shuttered record shop and answers letters by hand.

chapters.title: The Smile That Ends Conversations
chapters.summary: Oscar's POV. She mops the conservatory's practice halls at dawn, deflecting a young student who recognizes her name from old competition programs. Establishes her armor of cheerfulness and the scandal she refuses to name. Emotional beat: loneliness disguised as contentment.

chapters.title: Static and a Familiar Chord
chapters.summary: Oscar's POV. On a break, a radio in the loading dock plays a melody she knows was never recorded — her mentor Ilse Marchetti's 'Lullaby for the Unsent.' She drops a mop bucket, shattering the quiet. Emotional beat: the past arriving without permission.

chapters.title: Wendell Delivers
chapters.summary: Wendell's POV. A postal worker with a route through the conservatory, Wendell has delivered postcards to the fading memory of his late 'mother' figure, a retired accompanist, for ten years. He notices Oscar's reaction to the song. Emotional beat: two keepers of secrets recognizing each other.

chapters.title: Postcards to a Disappearing Woman
chapters.summary: Wendell's POV. He shows Oscar the postcards — written by Ilse before her death, addressed to the accompanist Marta, whose dementia erases her a little more each week. One card contains a sentence in Ilse's private notation. Emotional beat: tenderness entangled with grief.

chapters.title: The Untranslatable Sentence
chapters.summary: Oscar's POV. She attempts to decode the sentence, which mixes musical notation with a cipher Ilse taught her only once. It seems to reference 'the witness who recanted.' Oscar burns the first draft of her translation. Emotional beat: dread of what truth costs.

chapters.title: Who Owns a Song Never Recorded
chapters.summary: Oscar's POV. She investigates the radio broadcast and finds the station sourced the recording from a small archive — donated anonymously. The conservatory's new director, Dr. Voss, is curating an Ilse retrospective. Emotional beat: suspicion sharpening into purpose.

chapters.title: Voss's Clean Hands
chapters.summary: Oscar's POV, with a scene overheard. Dr. Voss is charming, ambitious, and was Ilse's last teaching assistant — the one who benefited from the scandal that ended Oscar's career. He offers Oscar a place in the retrospective, as 'a redeemed student.' Emotional beat: the smile that ends conversations nearly fails.

chapters.title: The Testimony File
chapters.summary: Wendell's POV. Wendell uses postal archives and a favor from a retired clerk to trace who mailed Ilse's papers after her death. The return address is Oscar's childhood home. Emotional beat: loyalty tested — Wendell wonders what Oscar is hiding.

chapters.title: What I Said at Nineteen
chapters.summary: Oscar's POV. Flashback chapter: at nineteen, pressured by Voss and the conservatory's lawyers, Oscar signed a statement claiming Ilse had stolen the piece from a student — a lie that destroyed Ilse's reputation and health. Emotional beat: shame surfacing after years underwater.

chapters.title: Marta Remembers a Tuesday
chapters.summary: Oscar and Wendell visit Marta, who briefly surfaces from dementia to describe the night Ilse played the Lullaby for the last time — and mentions 'the girl in the doorway.' Emotional beat: fragile clarity, more devastating than confusion.

chapters.title: The Archive Donation
chapters.summary: Wendell's POV. The donation trail leads to a shipping clerk who recalls a woman in a green coat — Voss's current assistant, Priya, who has been quietly leaking the recordings to radio, believing the music should outlive the politics. Emotional beat: unexpected ally.

chapters.title: Priya's Bargain
chapters.summary: Priya's POV. She reveals Voss plans to present the Lullaby as his own scholarly reconstruction, erasing Ilse's authorship and, with it, any reopening of the scandal. She'll help Oscar — if Oscar goes on record. Emotional beat: courage with strings attached.

chapters.title: The Sentence, Half-Translated
chapters.summary: Oscar's POV. The cipher finally yields: 'The one who lied knows the melody was mine, and silence is the theft's second verse.' Oscar plays the Lullaby alone at 3 a.m. in the practice hall, first time in twelve years. Emotional beat: grief and release braided together.

chapters.title: Vendetta in B Flat
chapters.summary: Oscar's POV. Voss discovers Oscar's inquiries and threatens to expose her janitorial past and her recantation, framing her as the villain of the story. He cancels her building access. Emotional beat: the institution closing ranks.

chapters.title: What Wendell Kept
chapters.summary: Wendell's POV. Wendell admits he has known Oscar's role for years — Marta told him long ago — and delivered Ilse's postcards anyway, waiting for Oscar to be ready. His loyalty was never blindness; it was patience. Emotional beat: forgiveness offered before it is asked.

chapters.title: The Postcard That Wasn't Sent
chapters.summary: Oscar's POV. Among the cards, one is addressed to Oscar herself, unsent: Ilse's last words to her, forgiving her and asking only that the music be played truthfully. Emotional beat: absolution arriving too late and exactly on time.

chapters.title: Rehearsal of Witnesses
chapters.summary: Oscar, Wendell, and Priya gather Marta, the retired clerk, and two former students. They plan to interrupt the retrospective gala with the true recording and Oscar's testimony. Emotional beat: a found family forming around a shared truth.

chapters.title: The Gala
chapters.summary: Oscar's POV. Voss unveils his 'reconstruction' before a full house. As the Lullaby plays, Oscar walks onstage in her janitor's uniform. Emotional beat: terror transmuted into resolve.

chapters.title: The Translation
chapters.summary: Oscar's POV, climax. She reads the translated sentence aloud, then her own recantation of the false testimony, naming Voss. The recording plays in full. Voss's career cracks publicly as the room turns. Emotional beat: the truth, spoken, finally lighter than the lie.

chapters.title: Aftermath, Mopped Floors
chapters.summary: Wendell's POV. The conservatory suspends the retrospective pending inquiry; Oscar resigns her post rather than be quietly absorbed back in. She and Wendell sort Ilse's remaining papers. Emotional beat: quiet aftermath, no applause needed.

chapters.title: Marta's Last Good Day
chapters.summary: Oscar's POV. Marta, in a rare lucid evening, hears the Lullaby played live by Priya and the students, and remembers Ilse whole. She calls Oscar 'the girl who came back.' Emotional beat: grace, brief and complete.

chapters.title: Lullaby for the Sent
chapters.summary: Oscar's POV. Months later, Oscar teaches a Saturday class for kids who can't afford the conservatory, in a room Wendell's postal friends helped furnish. She writes the first postcard of her own and mails it. Emotional beat: the melody continuing, honestly, in new hands.
